subject: Agriculture
title: China's Pork Empire
description: A quick win: understand China's Pork Empire.

hook.text: China has half the world's pigs—over 400 million. Pork is the foundation of Chinese cuisine.

buildup.text: The Chinese character for 'home' combines the symbols for roof and pig. Pigs define domesticity.

discovery.text: As China industrialized, backyard pigs moved to mega-farms with 100,000 animals under one roof.

twist.text: African swine fever killed a quarter of China's pigs in 2019—roughly 150 million animals wiped out.

climax.text: The loss spiked global pork prices and reshaped meat trade worldwide. One country's disease rattled markets.

punchline.text: When half the world's pigs sneeze, the global economy catches cold.

quiz.question: What happened to China's pig population in 2019?
options: African swine fever killed roughly a quarter—about 150 million pigs

details.summary: China produces and consumes half the world's pork, making its pork industry a global agricultural force. This topic covers China's rapid industrialization of pig farming, the devastating African swine fever outbreak, and the geopolitical impact of its pork demand.
details.whyItMatters: When African swine fever killed a quarter of China's pigs in 2018–2019, it reshaped global protein markets, drove up pork prices worldwide, and accelerated China's shift to industrial-scale mega-farms.
takeaways: China produces about 50 million tonnes of pork annually—half the global total
African swine fever killed roughly 200 million pigs in China during 2018–2019
China is building multi-story pig farms housing over 600,000 animals each

faq.question: Why is China so dominant in global pork production?
faq.answer: Pork is the traditional meat in Chinese cuisine, with per capita consumption among the highest globally. China has nearly 440 million pigs—more than the next 10 countries combined—supported by massive domestic soybean imports for feed.

faq.question: How did African swine fever impact China's pork industry?
faq.answer: The 2018–2019 outbreak killed or culled roughly 200 million pigs, reducing China's herd by about 40%. This caused a domestic pork price spike, massive imports from the US and Europe, and accelerated the shift from smallholder to industrial-scale farming.
